newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian opposition protests in bitter cold.
newsitem.headline: Serbian opposition protests in bitter cold.

text.p: Tens of thousands of demonstrators marched through Belgrade in bitter cold on Friday to express their anger towards President Slobodan Milosevic, who has refused to concede defeat in local elections.
The latest protest, in what has become a daily ritual of defiance against Milosevic's authoritarian rule, drew large numbers in Belgrade despite sleet and winter temperatures.
The crowd was slightly larger than the previous day, when an estimated 80,000 took to the streets.
Milosevic has chosen to ignore the demonstrations and his state media has portrayed the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition as outlaws and provocateurs.
Diplomats say Milosevic, whose police force has kept a low profile, was betting the demonstration campaign across the country would eventually run out of steam.
Zajedno organisers acknowledged the protests had peaked but said they had dealt a blow to Milosevic's image abroad.

"We have torn off his mask in front of the world to show him as he really is -- a small-time Balkan dictator unable to bear the slightest defeat," Zoran Djindjic, an opposition leader, told the crowd.
The wave of street protests, the biggest since 1991, came after the ruling Socialists annulled opposition victories in Belgrade and several other major towns, citing unspecified irregularities.
The opposition accused the Socialists of massive poll fraud and the United States has urged Milosevic to recognise the results of the secound round of municipal voting.
The Socialists organised a re-vote this week in Belgrade and other towns where Zajedno won. State media said the Socialists had secured a majority in the Belgrade city council.
A Belgrade court had earlier stripped Zajedno of a majority in the city council.
The opposition has threatened to call factory strikes but analysts said it lacks sufficient union support to organise a general strike that could pile pressure on Milosevic.

Many of those on the street said they did not believe Milosevic was about to fall but felt it was their duty to march. "I know this has very little chance of changing anything but what else can we do?" said one young woman.
The Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) said it was "extremely concerned" about irregularities during federal and municipal polls held earlier this month.
The OSCE said the integrity of the entire election process remained in doubt until an independent review could be conducted, offering to help if required.
The coalition said it planned to keep the protests rolling at least until Tuesday, when the Serbian parliament is due to convene.
Then they say Zajedno will surround the parliament with what they hope will be their biggest protest yet, to add weight to demands that the parliament recognise their "stolen" local election wins.
Diplomats say Milosevic has damaged his chances of rehabilitating himself in the West after moving to gag media coverage of the protests.

Belgrade's independent radio station B-92 said authorities jammed its news programme, while journalists from independent and state-backed newspapers have complained of attempts to censor their coverage of the protests.
